warmup.q: Two cook threads wait on an empty rail with if (rail.isEmpty()) lock.wait(); return rail.removeFirst();. A waiter thread adds one order and calls notifyAll() to wake the waiting cooks. What happens?
options: One cook gets the order and the other goes back to waiting
Both wake; one gets the order and the other throws NoSuchElementException
Neither wakes until a second order arrives
Both cooks get the same order
warmup.why: notifyAll() wakes both cooks, and they take the lock back one at a time. The first one takes the order. The second one checked its if before it went to sleep, so it calls removeFirst() on an empty rail, which throws NoSuchElementException. With while instead of if, it would check again and go back to waiting. The second section runs exactly this program.

opening:
Picture a restaurant kitchen. Waiters write each order on a ticket and clip it to a metal bar called the rail. Cooks take the oldest ticket off and cook it. When the rail is empty, a cook waits for the next ticket.

In a program, the rail is a queue (a list where items join at one end and leave from the other). Each waiter and each cook is a thread, a line of work that runs side by side with the others. The lock from the last lesson keeps the rail in order: one thread at a time touches it. But a lock says nothing about waiting. Most first versions either ask the empty rail "anything yet?" millions of times a second, or nap between looks and make each order wait for the nap to end.

Every Java object has a better answer, built into its lock. In this lesson, we'll teach a cook to wait for free, see why a second cook must check again, watch notify() stall the kitchen, and build the rail by hand. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a cook who had nothing to do but wait for the next ticket. We gave it a guarded block, a while loop for the second cook and notifyAll() for the rail with a limit, and built the rail by hand.

Now search your own code for .wait( and .await(. Each should sit in a while loop that tests a state. An if, or a wait with no condition, passes every test until the evening a second cook joins in.

Here, the stalled threads waited with the lock free. Next, we'll go back to the bank, where threads stop while holding locks: two transfers, each holding one account and waiting for the other. How does that happen, and how do you make sure it can't?

sections.h: Waiting for the rail without spinning: the guarded block
sections.html:
Let's start with one cook and an empty rail. The cook's thread must take the lock (with synchronized, as in the last lesson) every time it looks at the rail, since readers need the lock too. The quickest code just keeps looking:

Java
// Naive: asks the empty rail again and again
String nextOrder() {
    while (true) {
        synchronized (lock) {
            if (!rail.isEmpty()) return rail.removeFirst();
        }
    }
}
Kotlin
// Naive: asks the empty rail again and again
fun nextOrder(): String {
    while (true) {
        synchronized(lock) {
            if (rail.isNotEmpty()) return rail.removeFirst()
        }
    }
}

That loop is correct: it never takes an order that isn't there, and it never misses one. But it's a busy wait, or spin: a loop that checks the same thing again and again. The thread stays RUNNABLE (running, or ready to run) and keeps a processor core busy the whole time it waits. The waiters have to fight it for the lock every time they add an order.

The Try it below times a simpler spinner, which checks a volatile flag (a field that every thread always reads fresh), against a cook that waits properly. To wait one second, the spinning cook used about a full second of CPU time (time spent running on a processor). The waiting cook used 0 ms.

A Thread.sleep(50) between looks saves the CPU, but an order that lands just after a look then sits on the rail for up to 50 ms. A sleep is a guess about when the next order will arrive, and the guess is never quite right.

What we want is a cook that sleeps until the rail changes, and a waiter that wakes it when it does. Every Java object can do that, through its monitor, the built-in lock that synchronized takes. Here's the cook's side:

Java
// Fixed: sleeps until an order arrives
String nextOrder() throws InterruptedException {
    synchronized (lock) {
        while (rail.isEmpty()) {
            lock.wait();               // give back the lock, sleep until woken, take it again
        }
        return rail.removeFirst();     // the rail has an order, and we hold the lock
    }
}
Kotlin
// Fixed: sleeps until an order arrives
fun nextOrder(): String {
    synchronized(lock) {               // lock is a java.lang.Object: Kotlin's Any has no wait()
        while (rail.isEmpty()) {
            lock.wait()                // give back the lock, sleep until woken, take it again
        }
        return rail.removeFirst()      // the rail has an order, and we hold the lock
    }
}

wait() does three things, in order. First, it releases the monitor, so a waiter can get in. Then it parks the cook's thread, that is, puts it to sleep in the monitor's wait set, in the WAITING state, using no CPU. Finally, when the thread is woken, it takes the monitor back before wait() returns. So the line after wait() runs with the lock held, like the line before it.

A note on names, since this kitchen comes with a pun: here a waiter is always a person who carries orders, and a thread that has called wait() is a waiting thread.

A waiter does the other half, holding the same lock:

Java
void add(String order) {
    synchronized (lock) {
        rail.addLast(order);           // change the state first
        lock.notifyAll();              // then wake every thread waiting on lock
    }
}
Kotlin
fun add(order: String) {
    synchronized(lock) {
        rail.addLast(order)            // change the state first
        lock.notifyAll()               // then wake every thread waiting on lock
    }
}

notifyAll() wakes every thread in the wait set, but it doesn't hand over the lock. Each woken thread moves to the monitor's entry set, the threads lining up to get in. It shows as BLOCKED, the state of a thread waiting for a lock, until the waiter leaves its block. (Its sibling notify() wakes just one waiting thread. Which one it wakes will matter in the third section.)

Here's the same thing in the kitchen. The rail has one key, and only the thread holding the key may touch the rail. Threads that want the key stand in a line by the rail: that line is the entry set. A cook who finds the rail empty hangs the key back on its hook and sits on a bench at the back. The bench is the wait set. When a waiter clips a new ticket on, it rings the bell, and everyone on the bench gets up and joins the line for the key again. The bell is notifyAll(). The figure draws the line and the bench.

The cook's code is a guarded block. Its guard is a condition, a yes-or-no question about the shared state (here, "is there a ticket on the rail?"), and the thread waits until the answer is yes. Notice that the guard is a while, although with one cook an if looks just as good. We'll come back to that in the next section.

The order on the waiter's side matters too: state first, then the signal. If an order arrives before the cook starts waiting, the notifyAll() wakes nobody, and that's fine. The cook checks the rail first, finds the ticket and never calls wait(). Code that waits for a bare signal, with no state to check, sleeps forever when the signal comes first. That's a lost wake-up, and it passes tests because the waiting thread usually gets there first.

A notification is only a hint. Wait for a state, never for a signal.

One more rule holds it all together. You must hold the monitor of the object you call wait() or notifyAll() on, or you get IllegalMonitorStateException at once. Since the rail can change only under the lock, no order can slip in between the cook's check and its wait.

One cook now waits for free and wakes the moment an order lands. A busy evening needs a second one.

try.title: Spin vs wait
steps: Read BusyWaitDemo. Two cooks wait one second for the first order: the spinning cook checks a volatile flag over and over, and the waiting cook sits in a guarded block. Write down your guess for each thread's CPU time.
In the waiting cook, delete the synchronized line around the while loop and its closing brace, so lock.wait() runs without the lock. Predict what happens, run it, then put the lines back.

code.title: BusyWaitDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.concurrency.l05; import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory; import java.lang.management.ThreadMXBean; /** Two cooks wait one second for the first order. One spins, one calls wait(). Compare their CPU time. */ public class BusyWaitDemo { static final Object lock = new Object(); static boolean ready; // guarded by lock static volatile boolean readyForSpinner; // the spinner can't use the lock, so it needs volatile public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { Thread spinningCook = new Thread(() -> { while (!readyForSpinner) { } // busy-wait: checks the flag as fast as it can }, "spinning-cook"); Thread waitingCook = new Thread(() -> { synchronized (lock) { while (!ready) { // guarded block: the condition, in a loop try { lock.wait(); // releases lock, parks until notified } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); return; } } } }, "waiting-cook"); spinningCook.start(); waitingCook.start(); Thread.sleep(1_000); // the first order arrives a second later ThreadMXBean mx = ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean(); long spinCpu = mx.getThreadCpuTime(spinningCook.threadId()) / 1_000_000; // measure while both still wait long waitCpu = mx.getThreadCpuTime(waitingCook.threadId()) / 1_000_000; readyForSpinner = true; synchronized (lock) { ready = true; lock.notifyAll(); // wake the waiting cook; it runs once we leave this block } spinningCook.join(); waitingCook.join(); System.out.printf("the spinning cook used about %d ms of CPU to wait 1 s%n", spinCpu); System.out.printf("the waiting cook used about %d ms of CPU to wait 1 s%n", waitCpu); } }

alt.title: BusyWaitDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.concurrency.l05 import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory import kotlin.concurrent.thread // Two cooks wait one second for the first order. One spins, one calls wait(). Compare their CPU time. @Suppress("PLATFORM_CLASS_MAPPED_TO_KOTLIN") private val lock = Object() // java.lang.Object, because Kotlin's Any has no wait() private var ready = false // guarded by lock @Volatile private var readyForSpinner = false // the spinner can't use the lock, so it needs @Volatile fun main() { val spinningCook = thread(name = "spinning-cook") { while (!readyForSpinner) { } // busy-wait: checks the flag as fast as it can } val waitingCook = thread(name = "waiting-cook") { synchronized(lock) { while (!ready) { // guarded block: the condition, in a loop try { lock.wait() // releases lock, parks until notified } catch (e: InterruptedException) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt() return@thread } } } } Thread.sleep(1_000) // the first order arrives a second later val mx = ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean() val spinCpu = mx.getThreadCpuTime(spinningCook.threadId()) / 1_000_000 // measure while both still wait val waitCpu = mx.getThreadCpuTime(waitingCook.threadId()) / 1_000_000 readyForSpinner = true synchronized(lock) { ready = true lock.notifyAll() // wake the waiting cook; it runs once we leave this block } spinningCook.join() waitingCook.join() println("the spinning cook used about $spinCpu ms of CPU to wait 1 s") println("the waiting cook used about $waitCpu ms of CPU to wait 1 s") }

try.expect: The spinning cook uses about a full second of CPU to wait one second (runs here printed 992 to 1,037 ms). The waiting cook uses 0 ms. Without the synchronized block, the waiting cook dies at once with IllegalMonitorStateException: you can only wait on a monitor you hold.

aside.title: Why do the Kotlin samples lock on Object()?
aside.html: Kotlin's Any stands for java.lang.Object, but it doesn't expose wait(), notify() or notifyAll(). To call them, the Kotlin samples in this lesson declare the lock as a java.lang.Object itself, private val lock = Object(), which earns a compiler warning that the demos silence with @Suppress("PLATFORM_CLASS_MAPPED_TO_KOTLIN"). The usual Kotlin guarded block uses a ReentrantLock (a lock object you take and release by calling methods) and a Condition (a wait set of its own, attached to that lock) instead: await() plays the part of wait(), and signalAll() the part of notifyAll(). Every rule in this lesson holds there unchanged, and lesson 7 of this track covers it.

sections.h: A second cook, and why every wait sits in a while loop
sections.html:
Remember the while in the cook's guard? With one cook, an if seems to do the same job: check once, wait if the rail is empty, then take the ticket. Plenty of first versions look exactly like this:

Java
// Naive: checks once, before waiting
synchronized (lock) {
    if (rail.isEmpty()) lock.wait();
    return rail.removeFirst();
}
Kotlin
// Naive: checks once, before waiting
synchronized(lock) {
    if (rail.isEmpty()) lock.wait()
    return rail.removeFirst()
}

With one cook, that passes every test. So let's hire a second cook and send in a single order. The Try it below parks two cook threads in wait(), adds one order and calls notifyAll(). Here's what it printed:

cook-2 failed: java.util.NoSuchElementException
cook-1 took order-1

notifyAll() woke two cooks for one order, and the second one found the rail empty. NoSuchElementException is what removeFirst() throws when there is nothing to remove. Let's trace it, one thread at a time:

  1. Both cooks find the rail empty and call wait(), so both sit in the wait set.
  2. A waiter adds order-1 and calls notifyAll(). Both cooks move to the entry set.
  3. Cook 1 gets the lock first. Its wait() returns, it takes order-1, and it leaves.
  4. Cook 2 gets the lock next, and its wait() returns too. Its if ran long ago, before it waited, so it goes straight to removeFirst() on an empty rail.

Which cook wins, and which line prints first, changes from run to run. The ending doesn't.

With while, cook 2 checks the rail again after waking, finds it empty and goes back to waiting. Change that one word in the Try it, and the second cook waits quietly until main gives it order-2.

Being woken doesn't mean the state is right. Check again, in a while loop.

There's a second reason for the loop, in the Javadoc (the official API documentation) for Object.wait: "A thread can wake up without being notified, interrupted, or timing out, a so-called spurious wakeup." It's rare, but it's allowed, and the Javadoc tells you to test the condition again and keep waiting. In the kitchen, nobody gets up from the bench without hearing the bell; a Java thread is allowed to. So even a lone cook needs the loop. A second cook just makes the bug show up on the first busy evening.

The loop costs nothing, so use it every time. When you read code, treat an if around wait() as a bug, even in code that has never failed. It just hasn't had two cooks at once yet.

Two cooks now share the rail safely. But nothing stops the waiters from adding orders faster than the cooks can cook them. Next, we'll give the rail a limit, and the waiting starts on the other side too.

try.title: Steal a wake-up
steps: Read IfInsteadOfWhile. Both cooks are parked in wait() before main adds one order and calls notifyAll().
Run it and read both cooks' lines.
Change if (rail.isEmpty()) to while (rail.isEmpty()). Write down what you expect each cook to print, then run it again.

code.title: IfInsteadOfWhile.java
code.html: package workbench.concurrency.l05; import java.util.ArrayDeque; import java.util.Deque; /** Two cooks wait on an empty rail. One order arrives. The guard is an `if`. */ public class IfInsteadOfWhile { static final Object lock = new Object(); static final Deque<String> rail = new ArrayDeque<>(); static String take() throws InterruptedException { synchronized (lock) { if (rail.isEmpty()) { // BUG: checked once, never again after waking lock.wait(); } return rail.removeFirst(); // throws NoSuchElementException if someone else took it } } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { Runnable cook = () -> { try { System.out.println(Thread.currentThread().getName() + " took " + take()); } catch (Exception e) { System.out.println(Thread.currentThread().getName() + " failed: " + e); } }; Thread c1 = new Thread(cook, "cook-1"); Thread c2 = new Thread(cook, "cook-2"); c1.start(); c2.start(); while (c1.getState() != Thread.State.WAITING || c2.getState() != Thread.State.WAITING) { Thread.sleep(10); // wait until both are parked in wait() } synchronized (lock) { rail.addLast("order-1"); // one order... lock.notifyAll(); // ...and both cooks wake up } c1.join(2_000); c2.join(2_000); if (c1.isAlive() || c2.isAlive()) { // with `while`, one cook goes back to waiting System.out.println("one cook is still waiting; giving it a second order"); synchronized (lock) { rail.addLast("order-2"); lock.notifyAll(); } } c1.join(); c2.join(); } }

alt.title: IfInsteadOfWhile.kt
alt.html: package workbench.concurrency.l05 import java.util.ArrayDeque // Two cooks wait on an empty rail. One order arrives. The guard is an `if`. @Suppress("PLATFORM_CLASS_MAPPED_TO_KOTLIN") private val lock = Object() private val rail = ArrayDeque<String>() private fun take(): String { synchronized(lock) { if (rail.isEmpty()) { // BUG: checked once, never again after waking lock.wait() } return rail.removeFirst() // throws NoSuchElementException if someone else took it } } fun main() { val cook = Runnable { try { println("${Thread.currentThread().name} took ${take()}") } catch (e: Exception) { println("${Thread.currentThread().name} failed: $e") } } val c1 = Thread(cook, "cook-1") val c2 = Thread(cook, "cook-2") c1.start() c2.start() while (c1.state != Thread.State.WAITING || c2.state != Thread.State.WAITING) { Thread.sleep(10) // wait until both are parked in wait() } synchronized(lock) { rail.addLast("order-1") // one order... lock.notifyAll() // ...and both cooks wake up } c1.join(2_000) c2.join(2_000) if (c1.isAlive || c2.isAlive) { // with `while`, one cook goes back to waiting println("one cook is still waiting; giving it a second order") synchronized(lock) { rail.addLast("order-2") lock.notifyAll() } } c1.join() c2.join() }

try.expect: With if: one cook takes order-1 and the other fails with java.util.NoSuchElementException. With while: one cook takes order-1, the other checks again and goes back to waiting, main prints one cook is still waiting; giving it a second order, and that cook takes order-2. Which cook wins can change from run to run.

video.title: Two cooks, one ticket: the bell wakes both, so a woken cook checks the rail again in a while loop, and with two kinds of sleepers on one bench notify() can stall the kitchen

sections.h: A limit on the rail, and why notify() can stall it
sections.html:
So far only the cooks wait. When a big table orders twelve dishes at once, the cooks fall behind and the waiters keep adding tickets. A rail with no limit grows until the heap, the memory where Java keeps its objects, runs out. A real rail holds only so many tickets, so let's give ours a capacity, and make a waiter wait while it's full. At last, a job that suits the name:

Java
while (rail.size() == capacity) lock.wait();   // the waiter's guard: "not full"
Kotlin
while (rail.size == capacity) lock.wait()      // the waiter's guard: "not full"

A thread that puts work in is called a producer, and a thread that takes work out is a consumer: our waiters are producers, and our cooks are consumers. Making a fast producer wait for a slow consumer like this is called backpressure.

Backpressure also gives the monitor two kinds of waiting threads. Waiters wait for "not full", and cooks wait for "not empty". A monitor has only one wait set, so they all sit on the same bench.

With notifyAll(), that's harmless: everyone wakes, and each while loop sends back the threads that can't go on. With notify(), it isn't. notify() wakes one waiting thread, and it doesn't take requests: the JVM picks which one. Here's what that does to a rail with room for one ticket, two waiters and two cooks, where every signal is a notify():

  1. The rail is empty, so both cooks wait.
  2. Waiter 1 clips a ticket on, and its notify() wakes cook 1. Before cook 1 gets the lock, both waiters find the rail full and wait. The bench now holds waiter 1, waiter 2 and cook 2.
  3. Cook 1 takes the ticket and calls notify(), which happens to wake cook 2, the wrong kind.
  4. Cook 2 finds the rail empty and waits again. Cook 1 loops back, finds it empty too, and waits.

Now all four threads wait for a bell nobody is left to ring. No thread holds the lock, so this isn't a deadlock in the textbook sense (the next lesson has those), but the kitchen has stopped just the same. The Try it below gets there fast. One run printed:

using notify()
after 1 s: 8 orders cooked
stalled after 8 orders. Thread states:
  waiter-0: WAITING
  waiter-1: WAITING
  cook-0: WAITING
  cook-1: WAITING

Across runs here it stalled after 1 to 8 orders. With both signals switched to notifyAll(), the same four threads cooked about 136,000 to 139,000 orders in five seconds and never stalled. Each thread of the wrong kind checks its guard and goes back to waiting, so the right kind always gets a turn. The price is some extra wake-ups, which is cheap next to a stalled kitchen.

Two kinds of waiting threads on one monitor need notifyAll(). Wake them all, and let each loop decide.

notify() is safe only when every waiting thread waits for the same condition and one change lets at most one of them go on. Our rail with no limit, from the first two sections, qualified: only cooks waited, and one order let one cook go. A rail with a limit never does. For a precise wake-up per kind of waiting thread, give each kind its own Condition on a ReentrantLock, as lesson 7 of this track shows.

We now have all three pieces: a loop around every wait(), a change of state before every signal, and notifyAll() when the waiting threads differ. Let's put them together.

try.title: Stall a kitchen with notify()
steps: Run NotifyStall. Two waiters and two cooks share a rail with room for one ticket, and every signal is a notify().
When progress stops, read the thread states it prints and match them against the four steps in this section.
Predict whether it stalls with notifyAll(). Then run it again with -Pargs=all, which switches both signals to notifyAll().

code.title: NotifyStall.java
code.html: package workbench.concurrency.l05; import java.util.ArrayDeque; import java.util.Deque; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong; /** A rail with room for one order, shared by 2 waiters and 2 cooks. Uses notify(), or notifyAll() with -Pargs=all. */ public class NotifyStall { static final Object lock = new Object(); static final Deque<Integer> slot = new ArrayDeque<>(); static final AtomicLong moved = new AtomicLong(); static boolean all; // set once in main, before the threads start static void put(int x) throws InterruptedException { synchronized (lock) { while (!slot.isEmpty()) lock.wait(); slot.addLast(x); signal(); // notify() wakes ONE waiting thread: maybe a cook, maybe the other waiter } } static int take() throws InterruptedException { synchronized (lock) { while (slot.isEmpty()) lock.wait(); int x = slot.removeFirst(); signal(); return x; } } static void signal() { if (all) lock.notifyAll(); else lock.notify(); } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { all = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("all"); System.out.println(all ? "using notifyAll()" : "using notify()"); Thread[] threads = new Thread[4]; for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) { boolean producer = i < 2; threads[i] = new Thread(() -> { try { while (true) { if (producer) put(1); else { take(); moved.incrementAndGet(); } } } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } }, (producer ? "waiter-" : "cook-") + (i % 2)); threads[i].setDaemon(true); threads[i].start(); } long last = -1; for (int second = 1; second <= 5; second++) { Thread.sleep(1_000); long now = moved.get(); if (now == last) { System.out.printf("stalled after %,d orders. Thread states:%n", now); for (Thread t : threads) System.out.println(" " + t.getName() + ": " + t.getState()); return; } System.out.printf("after %d s: %,d orders cooked%n", second, now); last = now; } System.out.println(all ? "no stall: notifyAll() wakes every waiting thread, so the right kind always gets a turn" : "no stall this time; it depends on timing, so run it again"); } }

alt.title: NotifyStall.kt
alt.html: package workbench.concurrency.l05 import java.util.ArrayDeque import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong // A rail with room for one order, shared by 2 waiters and 2 cooks. Uses notify(), or notifyAll() with -Pargs=all. @Suppress("PLATFORM_CLASS_MAPPED_TO_KOTLIN") private val lock = Object() private val slot = ArrayDeque<Int>() private val moved = AtomicLong() private var all = false // set once in main, before the threads start private fun put(x: Int) { synchronized(lock) { while (!slot.isEmpty()) lock.wait() slot.addLast(x) signal() // notify() wakes ONE waiting thread: maybe a cook, maybe the other waiter } } private fun take(): Int { synchronized(lock) { while (slot.isEmpty()) lock.wait() val x = slot.removeFirst() signal() return x } } private fun signal() { if (all) lock.notifyAll() else lock.notify() } fun main(args: Array<String>) { all = args.firstOrNull() == "all" println(if (all) "using notifyAll()" else "using notify()") val threads = List(4) { i -> val producer = i < 2 Thread({ try { while (true) { if (producer) put(1) else { take(); moved.incrementAndGet() } } } catch (e: InterruptedException) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt() } }, (if (producer) "waiter-" else "cook-") + (i % 2)).apply { isDaemon = true start() } } var last = -1L for (second in 1..5) { Thread.sleep(1_000) val now = moved.get() if (now == last) { println("stalled after %,d orders. Thread states:".format(now)) threads.forEach { println(" ${it.name}: ${it.state}") } return } println("after %d s: %,d orders cooked".format(second, now)) last = now } println(if (all) "no stall: notifyAll() wakes every waiting thread, so the right kind always gets a turn" else "no stall this time; it depends on timing, so run it again") }

try.expect: With notify() it stalls almost at once (after 1 to 8 orders in runs here), with all four threads WAITING. With notifyAll() it never stalls, and cooks roughly 28,000 orders a second for the full five seconds. Your counts will differ. On a rare run notify() survives the five seconds; run it again, and it almost always stalls.

sections.h: The bounded buffer, built by hand, and where it stops
sections.html:
Put the three pieces together and you get the class you'll write in the lab: a bounded buffer, a queue with a fixed capacity that threads can share. It is our rail, written once for any kind of item. Waiters wait in put() when the cooks fall behind, and cooks wait in take() when there's nothing to cook:

Java
public class BoundedBuffer<T> {
    private final Object lock = new Object();
    private final Deque<T> items = new ArrayDeque<>();
    private final int capacity;

    public void put(T item) throws InterruptedException {
        synchronized (lock) {
            while (items.size() == capacity) {   // 1. guard: re-check after every wake-up
                lock.wait();
            }
            items.addLast(item);                 // 2. act: condition holds, lock held
            lock.notifyAll();                    // 3. signal: the state changed
        }
    }

    public T take() throws InterruptedException {
        synchronized (lock) {
            while (items.isEmpty()) {
                lock.wait();
            }
            T head = items.removeFirst();
            lock.notifyAll();
            return head;
        }
    }
}
Kotlin
class BoundedBuffer<T>(private val capacity: Int) {
    @Suppress("PLATFORM_CLASS_MAPPED_TO_KOTLIN")
    private val lock = Object()                    // java.lang.Object: Kotlin's Any has no wait()
    private val items = ArrayDeque<T>()

    @Throws(InterruptedException::class)           // so Java callers see it, as in the Java version
    fun put(item: T) {
        synchronized(lock) {
            while (items.size == capacity) {       // 1. guard: re-check after every wake-up
                lock.wait()
            }
            items.addLast(item)                    // 2. act: condition holds, lock held
            lock.notifyAll()                       // 3. signal: the state changed
        }
    }

    @Throws(InterruptedException::class)
    fun take(): T {
        synchronized(lock) {
            while (items.isEmpty()) {
                lock.wait()
            }
            val head = items.removeFirst()
            lock.notifyAll()
            return head
        }
    }
}

put() and take() have the same three parts. The guard is the while loop that waits until the method can go on. The act changes the rail, safely, because the condition holds and the lock is held. The signal wakes the other side, because the state it waits on just changed. Read put() aloud and it says: while there's no room, wait; add the item; tell everyone something changed.

Three smaller choices are deliberate, and each comes from an earlier lesson. The lock is a private object, as synchronized and intrinsic locks recommended, so only the buffer can wait on it or signal it. Both methods signal with notifyAll(), because producers and consumers share one wait set. And both declare throws InterruptedException, the exception a waiting thread gets when another thread interrupts it, that is, asks it to stop. The buffer can't know what its caller wants to do about an interrupt, so it lets the exception propagate, that is, pass up to the caller. That's one of the two good answers from A thread's life.

Now the honest part. In real code you won't write this class: ArrayBlockingQueue from the JDK does the same job, with timeouts, and lesson 9 of this track covers it. Our buffer also has a cost built in. With one wait set, every notifyAll() wakes producers and consumers alike, and most of them check their guard and go straight back to waiting. A Condition gives one lock a separate wait set per condition, and lesson 7 of this track builds on that.

Why build it, then? Because guarded blocks hide inside many libraries you'll use. If you write programs that use a database, for example, you'll meet a connection pool: a fixed set of open database connections that threads borrow and give back. A pool of 20 makes the 21st thread wait in a guarded block until a connection comes back. In a thread dump, a printout of every thread's state and the method calls it is in the middle of, those threads show WAITING or TIMED_WAITING inside the library's code. Once you've written put() and take() yourself, you can tell which condition they wait for.

Check your model before you start the lab. Delete the notifyAll() in take(). Two waiters fill a rail of capacity 2 and then wait in put(). A cook takes one order. What happens next? (The waiters stay in wait(): the take made room, but nothing woke them. The cooks empty the rail and then wait too, until every thread is waiting.)

compare.title: A guarded buffer in Java and Kotlin

java.title: BoundedBuffer.java
java.html: public class BoundedBuffer<T> { private final Object lock = new Object(); private final Deque<T> items = new ArrayDeque<>(); private final int capacity; public void put(T item) throws InterruptedException { synchronized (lock) { while (items.size() == capacity) { // 1. guard: re-check after every wake-up lock.wait(); } items.addLast(item); // 2. act: condition holds, lock held lock.notifyAll(); // 3. signal: the state changed } } public T take() throws InterruptedException { synchronized (lock) { while (items.isEmpty()) { lock.wait(); } T head = items.removeFirst(); lock.notifyAll(); return head; } } }

kotlin.title: KotlinGuarded.kt
kotlin.html: package workbench.concurrency.l05 import java.util.ArrayDeque import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock import kotlin.concurrent.thread import kotlin.concurrent.withLock // Kotlin's Any has no wait()/notify(). The idiomatic guarded block uses a Lock and a Condition. class KotlinBuffer<T>(private val capacity: Int) { private val lock = ReentrantLock() private val changed = lock.newCondition() // one wait set, like a monitor's private val items = ArrayDeque<T>() fun put(item: T) = lock.withLock { while (items.size == capacity) changed.await() // same while-loop guard items.addLast(item) changed.signalAll() // same as notifyAll() } fun take(): T = lock.withLock { while (items.isEmpty()) changed.await() items.removeFirst().also { changed.signalAll() } } } fun main() { val buffer = KotlinBuffer<Int>(2) val consumer = thread { repeat(5) { println("took ${buffer.take()}") } } repeat(5) { buffer.put(it) } consumer.join() }

compare.note: Both versions are the same guarded buffer: the same while guard, the same act, and the same signal to every waiting thread. Three things changed in the Kotlin one. lock.withLock { } takes and releases a ReentrantLock where Java writes synchronized. changed.await() stands in for wait(). And changed.signalAll() stands in for notifyAll(). The Java version uses the monitor that every object has carried since Java 1.0, and it needs nothing else. The Kotlin version reaches for a Condition because Kotlin's Any doesn't expose wait(). The rules don't change with the tool: Condition allows spurious wakeups too, so the while stays. What the Condition adds is room to grow, because one lock can have several conditions, so producers and consumers could wait separately. Lesson 7 of this track builds exactly that.

worked.title: Wait for a dish, with a deadline

steps.say: A waiter thread waits until the kitchen marks a table's dish as ready. After 30 seconds it gives up, so it can go and tell the table about the delay. Here is the first attempt. Before you read on, find what can go wrong.
steps.code: boolean awaitDish() throws InterruptedException { synchronized (lock) { if (!dishReady) lock.wait(30_000); return dishReady; } }

alt.html: fun awaitDish(): Boolean { synchronized(lock) { if (!dishReady) lock.wait(30_000) return dishReady } }

steps.say: It's the if bug in a new shape. wait(30_000) waits at most 30 seconds, but it can return sooner. A spurious wakeup, or a notifyAll() meant for some other condition on the same lock, makes wait() return early with dishReady still false: after 2 seconds, say, instead of 30. Just moving wait(30_000) into a while loop is wrong too, because every wake-up would start a fresh 30 seconds. The cure is to set the deadline once and wait only for what's left of it.
The guard loop now checks two things: the condition and the clock. Each pass waits only for the time that's left.
steps.code: boolean awaitDish(Duration timeout) throws InterruptedException { long deadline = System.nanoTime() + timeout.toNanos(); // 1. fix the deadline once synchronized (lock) { while (!dishReady) { // 2. guard on the condition long leftMillis = (deadline - System.nanoTime()) / 1_000_000; if (leftMillis <= 0) return false; // 3. out of time lock.wait(leftMillis); // 4. wait only for what's left } return true; } }

alt.html: fun awaitDish(timeout: Duration): Boolean { val deadline = System.nanoTime() + timeout.toNanos() // 1. fix the deadline once synchronized(lock) { while (!dishReady) { // 2. guard on the condition val leftMillis = (deadline - System.nanoTime()) / 1_000_000 if (leftMillis <= 0) return false // 3. out of time lock.wait(leftMillis) // 4. wait only for what's left } return true } }

steps.say: The cook's thread sets the state before it signals, both under the lock, just as the waiters did with the rail. If it runs before anyone waits, nothing is lost: the waiter thread sees dishReady and never calls wait(). One question before the last step: why does the waiter use System.nanoTime() and not System.currentTimeMillis()?
steps.code: void onDishReady() { synchronized (lock) { dishReady = true; // state first lock.notifyAll(); // then the signal } }

alt.html: fun onDishReady() { synchronized(lock) { dishReady = true // state first lock.notifyAll() // then the signal } }

steps.say: nanoTime() only ever moves forward, so it measures elapsed time. currentTimeMillis() is the wall-clock time, and the computer may move it backwards or forwards when it corrects its clock over the network (with a service called NTP), which would stretch or cut the timeout.

lab.title: Build a bounded buffer with wait and notifyAll
steps: Meet the class. BoundedBuffer is this lesson's rail, written for any type of item: put adds at the tail and waits while the buffer is full, and take removes from the head and waits while it's empty.
Run the tests. All six fail, some only after a few seconds, because the threads that should wait die instead.
Add the fields: a private lock object, an ArrayDeque for the items, the capacity. Reject a capacity below 1 in the constructor.
Write put: guard with while (full) lock.wait();, add at the tail, then notifyAll().
Write take: guard with while (empty) lock.wait();, remove the head, notifyAll(), and return it. Write size() under the lock.
Run the tests until all six pass, then twice more. The test with four producers and four consumers is the one that catches if and notify() mistakes.
hints: The blocking tests poll getState() until it says WAITING. A thread that sleeps in a loop shows TIMED_WAITING and fails them. Use wait() with no timeout.
Call wait() and notifyAll() on the same object you synchronize on. Calling wait() on this while holding lock throws IllegalMonitorStateException.
Don't catch InterruptedException inside the buffer. Let it propagate: both methods already declare it.
lab.done: All six tests in BoundedBufferTest pass, three runs in a row.

drill.title: A bounded buffer from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page and the lab. In a blank file, write a bounded buffer of String with put and take, using synchronized, wait and notifyAll. Then check your work: is every wait() inside a while? Do both methods signal? Did you lock on a private object?

answer.html: public class BoundedBuffer<T> { private final Object lock = new Object(); private final Deque<T> items = new ArrayDeque<>(); private final int capacity; public void put(T item) throws InterruptedException { synchronized (lock) { while (items.size() == capacity) { // 1. guard: re-check after every wake-up lock.wait(); } items.addLast(item); // 2. act: condition holds, lock held lock.notifyAll(); // 3. signal: the state changed } } public T take() throws InterruptedException { synchronized (lock) { while (items.isEmpty()) { lock.wait(); } T head = items.removeFirst(); lock.notifyAll(); return head; } } }

alt.title: Kotlin
alt.html: class BoundedBuffer<T>(private val capacity: Int) { @Suppress("PLATFORM_CLASS_MAPPED_TO_KOTLIN") private val lock = Object() // java.lang.Object: Kotlin's Any has no wait() private val items = ArrayDeque<T>() @Throws(InterruptedException::class) // so Java callers see it, as in the Java version fun put(item: T) { synchronized(lock) { while (items.size == capacity) { // 1. guard: re-check after every wake-up lock.wait() } items.addLast(item) // 2. act: condition holds, lock held lock.notifyAll() // 3. signal: the state changed } } @Throws(InterruptedException::class) fun take(): T { synchronized(lock) { while (items.isEmpty()) { lock.wait() } val head = items.removeFirst() lock.notifyAll() return head } } }

recap: A guarded block holds the lock, checks a condition, and calls wait() until the condition holds. wait() gives the monitor back while it waits and takes it again before it returns.
Call wait(), notify() or notifyAll() only while holding that object's monitor, or you get IllegalMonitorStateException.
Always while (!condition) wait();. Another woken thread may change the state before you get the lock back, and spurious wakeups are allowed.
Change the state, then notify. Wait for a state, never for a bare signal, so an early notification is never lost.
notify() wakes one waiting thread of the JVM's choosing. With two kinds of waiting threads on one monitor it can wake the wrong kind and stall everything, so default to notifyAll().

The limit: a monitor has one wait set, so every notifyAll() wakes every kind of waiting thread. A Condition gives each kind its own (lesson 7), and ArrayBlockingQueue does the whole job for you (lesson 9).

explain.prompt: Explain to a friend who is new to threads why a bounded buffer built on one monitor needs while loops and notifyAll(), and what goes wrong if you use if or notify() instead.
explain.answer: Producers wait for "not full" and consumers wait for "not empty", but with one monitor they share one wait set. When a thread wakes, the state may already have changed again, because other woken threads can get the lock first, and spurious wakeups are allowed. So each waiting thread must check its condition again in a while loop. With if, a consumer can wake up and remove from an empty buffer. notify() wakes one waiting thread of the JVM's choosing, which may be the wrong kind: a consumer waking another consumer wastes the only signal, and soon every thread waits with nobody left to wake them. notifyAll() wakes everyone, and the loops send the ones that can't go on back to waiting.

deeper.html:
Timed waits are the same idea with a clock. wait(millis) returns when it's notified, interrupted, woken spuriously, or when the time is up, and it doesn't tell you which. That's why the worked example tracks its own deadline with System.nanoTime().

The JVM has had bugs here too. JDK 26 carries a fix titled "Notification can be lost due to interrupt in Object.wait". That's one more reason to use the standard library's queues and synchronizers wherever you can: they are tested far harder than any guarded block you or I will write.

Two notes on observing waits. Java Flight Recorder (JFR), the event recorder built into the JVM, has a jdk.JavaMonitorWait event, with the monitor's class, the thread that notified, the timeout and whether it timed out, and JDK 25 added a jdk.JavaMonitorNotify event. And on virtual threads (very light threads that the JVM runs on top of a few ordinary carrier threads), Object.wait() used to pin, that is, hold on to, the carrier thread. Since JDK 24 (JEP 491) it no longer does in most cases.

Finally, the history. wait and notify have been in Java since 1.0. java.util.concurrent arrived in Java 5 with Condition, BlockingQueue and friends, built by Doug Lea on a framework called AbstractQueuedSynchronizer. Read the source of ArrayBlockingQueue and you'll find the same guard, act and signal as in this lesson, written with a ReentrantLock and two Conditions.
